title: Taking Managed Instances through design, security and rollout
question: Tell me about a time you drove a technical initiative

situation: AWS launched Managed Instances for Lambda so customers could run functions on EC2 infrastructure with native scaling and cost efficiency. As part of the Code Management & Optimization team, our service had to support function packaging, artifact storage and optimisation for this new execution tier.
task: I took ownership of my team's initiative: leading the high-level design and the operational readiness review, driving the multi-service deployment, and acting as a technical point of contact for the control plane and data plane partner teams.
action: High-level design ownership: with limited input from the global tech lead, I was effectively the source for our team's high-level design, shaping the initial architecture.

Architectural steering and pivot: my first design aimed to stay as closely aligned with Lambda On-Demand as possible, ideally allowing an easy switch between the two. About two months in, with roughly 75% of the work done, I started questioning that direction, and following the best security recommendations for artifact movement, identified that dedicated artifact encryption at rest was the stronger long-term solution, even though it meant giving up that alignment. I drove the shift, re-architected the design, and rewrote the core components before it could become a blocker.

Cross-service delivery: I guided integration of our team's piece with several control plane and data plane dependencies, driving a zero-customer-impact deployment on our side and establishing rigorous validation pipelines along the way.
result: All of the team's code changes and operational readiness requirements landed on schedule with zero customer impact, giving Lambda Managed Instances seamless support from our service.

challenge: Pivoting a design that was already 75% built. Recognising on my own initiative that dedicated artifact encryption at rest was the stronger long-term choice, even though it meant giving up full Lambda On-Demand alignment, meant revisiting our fundamental data flows and rewriting a large part of the codebase under a tight timeline, well after the original direction was largely in place.
hardestBug: Cross-service failure scenarios during joint testing. Our code interacted with several external control and data plane services, so I regularly had to run exhaustive isolation tests to pinpoint edge-case failures and demonstrate to partner teams that the fault lay in their service layer.
differently: I would push for an explicit early audit of emerging security and compliance requirements, rather than assuming a new feature paradigm can align fully with legacy execution patterns like Lambda On-Demand.
aboutYourself: I have the technical depth and confidence to drive my team's piece of a major initiative end to end, even when it meant influencing decisions beyond my own team's boundaries. It showed me I can challenge flawed assumptions and pivot a high-level design without giving up the timeline.
enjoyed: Mapping out the end-to-end system design, finding the subtle edge cases, and reasoning through complex multi-service interactions across the AWS control and data plane ecosystem.
